newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power seen down amid high runoff.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power seen down amid high runoff.

text.p: Expectations for much above normal runoff at hydroelectric projects in the U.S. West this year translate into lower spot power prices, industry sources said Thursday.
"You wouldn't want to pay very much. You might even want to be a little short," said one West Coast industry source.
"A lot of cheap energy will be out there," he added.
The National Weather Service's Northwest River Forecast Center in Portland, Ore., released Thursday its first official monthly forecast for January-July runoff.

Runoff at The Dalles, the second-to-last hydroelectric dam on the Columbia River in Oregon, is now expected to reach 130 percent of a 30-year average, compared with actual flows last year at 132 percent of average.
Runoff at The Dalles was 98 percent of normal levels in 1995 and 71 percent in 1994.

The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), the federal agency which markets hydropower from federal dams in the Northwest, this week began offering power as low as $7.00 per megawatt (MWh) for buyers willing to displace generation from thermal sources such as natural gas-fired plants.
Last spring, BPA offered displacement power as low as $3.00 per MWh.
California hydropower output is also expected to hit high levels this year, with statewide snowpack water volume assessed near 140 percent of normal for this time of year.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, hydropower accounted for nearly 70 percent of total generation for Washington, Oregon and California in the first nine months of last year, up from around 65 percent in the same 1995 period.

The mountain states, the census division which includes the other states in the western power grid, saw 18 percent of total generation from hydropower in January-September of last year, compared with 14 percent in the same 1995 period.
Industry sources noted, however, that issues such as fish migration or an unexpected freeze could affect dam operations over the next few months.
Nevertheless, "it is unlikely at this point that the water situation will change that much," said another market source.
